title: Peregrine Aero — Edge Ops & Terraform compatibility notes (draft)
body:
Summary:
This note captures the current assumptions, terraform module compatibility considerations, and a pragmatic upgrade/cutover plan for Peregrine Aero's private inference installation across 3 hangars + central data room. Intended as an engineering-facing draft for the SOW and infra ticketing; content is intentionally operational and contains TODOs for final sizing sign-off.

Context / goals:
- Customer: Peregrine Aero (avionics analytics + pilot-assist features).
- Objective: Deliver a private deployment (VPC + on-prem racks) that runs Redwood inference runtime for low-latency cockpit features and batch analytics for maintenance.
- Constraints: intermittent site connectivity, strict FIPS-aligned KMS requirements, limited cooling in Hangar B, and existing on-prem VMware footprint in central data room.
- RTO target: 5m for control-plane failover; P99 inference latency target: 80–120ms for small models, 300–600ms for large generative models.

Key workload assumptions (draft numbers — customer confirmation required):
- Steady-state active sessions: 200 concurrent low-latency assistant sessions across hangars (avg. request size 128 tokens/request).
- Peak batch jobs (nightly): 12 concurrent large-model evaluation jobs (up to 4096 token sequences).
- Expected model mix: 60% 4-bit quantized medium LLMs (7–13B), 30% fp16 worker for legacy 65B model, 10% occasional H100-class ops for research.
- Target utilization: max GPU util 70% steady-state, allow 15% headroom for spiky telemetry.
- Network egress between hangars and central: 1 Gbps redundant links; prefer to keep inference traffic local to hangar when latency-bound.

Recommended physical layout and Sizing (initial proposal):
- Hangar nodes (x3 hangars): each hangar: 2x GPU nodes (A10G equivalent) + 2x CPU-only control nodes. Rationale: distributed low-latency capacity near devices, cheap to scale horizontally.
- Central data room: 4x larger GPU nodes (4x H100/8x A100 equivalent) for batch, heavy models, and central control plane services.
- Storage: NFS backed by on-prem NAS for artifacts; local NVMe on GPU nodes for KV cache + model shard caching. Plan for 2TB NVMe per GPU node.
- Network: FLAT L2 overlay between hangars for low-latency RPC; provision dedicated VLAN for inference control-plane and separate for telemetry.

Cost/Capacity table (rough):
- Hangar (per hangar): 2x A10G nodes, 48 vCPU, 384 GB RAM — supports ~70 concurrent small-model sessions each.
- Central: 4x H100-class nodes — supports async batch and large-model fallbacks.

Terraform & infra notes (compatibility and module suggestions):
- Use dedicated repo branch: terraform-modules/edge-deploy/peregrine-2025. Keep remote state in S3-compatible object store in central data room (minio), encrypted with customer KMS.
- Modules to reuse: ri-vpc (adapted), ri-iam (locks down service accounts), ri-gpu-node (small wrapper around provider-specific instance + local NVMe attachment), ri-lb (internal NLB for control-plane).
- Providers: aws (for any cloud-managed connectivity), vsphere (central VMware), local-exec to call cluster bootstrap scripts.
- Workspaces: one workspace per site (hangar-a, hangar-b, hangar-c, central). Avoid using a single workspace across all sites to reduce blast radius.
- Remote state locking: enabled via DynamoDB-style locking in the object store; if not available, use consul or apply sequential approvals.
- State drift: create a scheduled weekly `terraform plan` CI job that posts drift summaries to Slack and a central S3 bucket.
- Immutable tags: set tags on all created infra with customer identifier, deployment-phase, and created_by.

Cluster and runtime integration notes (Redwood runtime):
- kube vs baremetal: prefer k8s for central room (to support batch pods and autoscaling); hangar node pools are simpler single-tenant docker-compose/baremetal runtime to reduce orchestration overhead and handling of intermittent connectivity.
- Model artifacts: central artifact registry with hashed manifests. Hangar nodes pull manifests and store models locally; implement a TTL eviction for cold models (configurable).
- KV cache: use persisted on-host cache in NVMe; ensure consistent path across node images for smooth upgrades.
- Batching config: conservative batching in hangars (max batch size 12, target latency 120ms) and aggressive in central (batch size 64 for throughput jobs).

Upgrade & Cutover plan (minimal risk strategy):
1) Prep: create infra branch, confirm KMS access, validate network VLANs, snapshot existing VMs and back up current configs (full export).
2) Staging: deploy full stack into a staged hangar (replica environment) using workspace hangar-staging. Run smoke tests and perf benchmarks with synthetic workloads reflecting production mix.
3) Canary: pick Hangar A; deploy new operator and runtime in canary mode (traffic split 10/90 from old runtime). Monitor p99/p95 latency and token error rates for 24h.
4) Incremental rollout: if stable, increment traffic to 50% then 100% over rolling 12h windows. Maintain rollback snapshots for each increment.
5) Central migration: once hangars stable, migrate central components during a low-usage window; use blue/green for batch systems to avoid job loss.
6) Post-upgrade: run full e2e validation suite including sample cockpit interactions, offline job integrity checks, and model quality smoke tests.
7) Rollback procedure: terraform rollback using stored state snapshot from before the canary plus restore of model cache snapshot. For single-node failures use local node drain then rebuild from scratch nodes.

Operational runbooks and checks (quick list):
- Preflight checklist: time-sync, KMS key access, DNS entries, firewall routes, NVMe health, node temps.
- Post-deploy checks: service heartbeats, model pull success rate, KV cache hit %, avg batch latency, token reject rate.
- Monitoring: expose per-model latency, per-node GPU util, disk eviction rate. Hook alerts into SRE Slack and PagerDuty.

Open questions for Peregrine (to surface in SOW):
- Confirm approved GPU families (A10G vs A100/H100) and procurement timeline.
- Are hangar networks allowed to have cross-hangar multicast/overlay? If not, we must adopt a pull model for artifacts only.
- KMS: customer-managed HSM or Redwood-managed key with HSM export control?
- Do they require air-gapped install variant for any hangar (no external artifact pull allowed)?

Known risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Hangar B cooling limits reduce sustained GPU performance. Mitigation: leverage central fallback for heavy models and rate-limit local ops during heat windows.
- Risk: Terraform state exposure in central object store. Mitigation: server-side encryption + customer KMS + strict ACLs.
- Risk: Model quality regressions after a runtime upgrade. Mitigation: holdback model-compatibility tests in staging and do basic evals on a small labeled prompt set before canary.

Action items / TODOs (owner assignment):
- [Diego] Finalize vm/gpu SKU choices with procurement (due 2025-02-17).
- [Priya] Draft SOW appendix on KMS and encryption (due 2025-02-20).
- [Lina] Create terraform repo branch and initial workspace scaffolding (due 2025-02-24).
- [Marcus] Prep staged hangar and run smoke tests (due 2025-02-28).

Appendix: helpful terraform snippets (pointer only)
- resource "ri_gpu_node" "hangar_a_gpu" {
    provider = vsphere
    sku = "a10g-48g"
    nvme_size_gb = 2000
    tags = ["peregrine","hangar-a"]
  }
- state backend example:
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = "peregrine-terraform-state"
    key    = "hangar-a/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "local"
    encrypt = true
  }

End of draft.

Feedback welcome — this is intentionally operational and incomplete; please add concrete SKU approvals and network diagrams to the staged Confluence page linked above.
